deck: 20 Head First Java::04 How Objects Behave

cards.front: A class has state and behaviour. What do its methods usually act on?
cards.extra: Behaviour reads and changes state: a Dog barks differently because its size field differs. That interaction is what makes the object more than a struct.

cards.front: You pass an int to a method and the method changes the parameter. What does the caller see?
cards.extra: Java passes primitives by value, always. Assigning a new value inside the method changes only the local copy, never the caller's variable.

cards.front: You pass an object reference to a method and the method changes a field through it. What does the caller see?
cards.back: The change — both references point at the same object
cards.extra: The reference is still passed by value (a copy of the pointer), but copying a remote control does not copy the TV. That distinction is the source of the "Java is pass-by-reference" myth.

cards.front: What does void in a method signature mean?
cards.extra: You can still return; to leave early. A method that promises a type must return a value of that type on every path, or it will not compile.

cards.front: How does a method hand a value back to its caller?
cards.back: With a return expression matching the declared type
cards.extra: int giveSecret() { return 42; } — the declared type is a contract. Returning something incompatible is a compile error.

cards.front: What is encapsulation in its concrete form?
cards.extra: The fields are hidden behind methods, so every read and write goes through code you control. That is the whole mechanism; the theory follows from it.

cards.front: Why does private plus a setter beat a public field?
cards.back: The setter can validate; direct assignment cannot
cards.extra: A setter can reject, clamp or transform a value — as in refusing a negative height. With a public field, any caller can write a value that breaks the object's invariant, and nothing runs in between.

cards.front: An object's field is never assigned. What does it hold?
cards.extra: Instance variables are initialised by the JVM, so a new object's fields are never undefined — they are zero-ish. That is why a fresh object prints 0 and null.

cards.front: A local variable is declared but never assigned. What does it hold?
cards.back: Nothing — reading it is a compile error
cards.extra: The compiler refuses with "variable x might not have been initialized". Locals have no default, unlike fields; the compiler forces you to assign before use.

cards.back: The bits: a value for primitives, an identity for references
cards.extra: It never looks inside an object. Two different Integer objects holding 1000 are not ==; two references to the same object always are.

cards.front: When does == work on objects and when does it mislead?
cards.back: Works when you mean same object; misleads when you mean same contents
cards.extra: Use .equals() for value equality on Strings, wrappers and your own types. == on two separately built strings is almost always a bug.

cards.back: The array element, which holds a reference to a Dog object
cards.extra: Indexing returns the reference stored in the slot, then the dot calls the method on that object. The array is a tray of remote controls, not a tray of dogs.

cards.front: How does a method receive input?
cards.back: Through parameters in its signature; the caller supplies arguments
cards.extra: void bark(int numOfBarks) declares one parameter; d.bark(3) passes the argument 3, which is copied into the parameter. The method can only change its own copy.

cards.front: What must the argument count and types match?
cards.back: The method's parameters, or it will not compile
cards.extra: bark() and bark(int) are different methods, so the call decides which one runs. Widening is allowed (an int fits a long parameter); narrowing needs a cast.
